priorites.intro: A simple guide to what to do first when things go wrong.
etapes: 3 minutes without air: clearing the airway and stopping a haemorrhage are the absolute priority.
3 hours without shelter in cold, wet weather or great heat: protect yourself before looking for food.
3 days without water: finding water and making it safe comes next.
3 weeks without food: on a bivouac of a few days, food is never the emergency.
Keep a cool head: stop, think, observe, plan (the “STOP” of survival manuals).
attention: These durations are orders of magnitude, not limits to test.
priorites.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

eau.intro: Even when clear, river water can contain bacteria and parasites (farms and villages upstream). Boiling is the only truly safe improvised method.
etapes: Pre-filter through a clean cloth to remove particles.
Bring to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m).
Let it cool covered, in a clean container.
Without a fire: a certified hiking filter or purification tablets, respecting the stated waiting time.
Draw water upstream of the camp, away from pastures and stagnant water.
attention: Boiling doesn't remove chemical pollutants: avoid water near treated fields, roads or industrial sites.
eau.source: WHO; review “Improvised Water Procurement in Wilderness Medicine” (medRxiv, 2025)

filtre.intro: Clears cloudy water before boiling it. It does NOT make it drinkable on its own.
etapes: Cut off the bottom of a plastic bottle and turn it upside down, cap slightly unscrewed or pierced.
Stack from bottom to top: crushed charcoal (from last night's fire, without ash), fine sand, gravel, then cloth or grass.
Pour the water slowly in from the top and throw away the first runs, which are often still cloudy.
Boil the filtered water for 1 minute before drinking it.
attention: No study shows that a home-made filter removes germs: always boil afterwards.
filtre.source: WHO; review “Improvised Water Procurement in Wilderness Medicine” (medRxiv, 2025)

pluie.intro: The best improvised source: a few litres per shower for very little effort.
etapes: Stretch a tarp, poncho or survival blanket sloping towards a low point.
Put a clean container under that low point (bottle, pot, dry bag).
Let the first rain rinse the tarp before collecting.
Store it under cover and boil it if the water has stood or touched leaves.
pluie.source: WHO; review “Improvised Water Procurement in Wilderness Medicine” (medRxiv, 2025)

transpiration.intro: A clear plastic bag over a leafy branch collects the water the plant gives off. Useful in sun, weak in November.
etapes: Choose a leafy branch of a NON-poisonous tree or shrub, well exposed to the sun.
Slip a clear plastic bag over it and close it tightly around the branch.
Let one corner of the bag hang down, with a small pebble inside to create a low point.
Collect at the end of the day by piercing the corner or opening the bag, then change branch.
attention: Yield from a few decilitres to 1 litre a day, and only in fine weather.
Never on yew, foxglove, bittersweet or an unidentified plant.
transpiration.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain); WHO; review “Improvised Water Procurement in Wilderness Medicine” (medRxiv, 2025)

rosee.intro: An extra top-up, early in the morning, when the grass is soaked.
etapes: Just before sunrise, tie an absorbent cloth (T-shirt, rag) around your ankles or hold it in your hand.
Walk through or drag it in tall wet grass.
Wring it out regularly into a container.
Boil before drinking.
attention: Very low yield (about a glass): never count on it as a main source.
rosee.source: WHO; review “Improvised Water Procurement in Wilderness Medicine” (medRxiv, 2025)

feu.intro: 90% of failed fires fail for lack of preparation. Fires in forests are tightly controlled: in Wallonia, forbidden except at designated spots; in France, forbidden in woods and within 200 m of them for anyone who isn't the owner. Check the local rules.
etapes: Choose an allowed spot, sheltered from the wind, cleared of leaves and away from roots and low branches.
Gather a big handful of tinder: birch bark (burns even when damp), dry grass, dead needles, fine shavings.
Prepare the kindling in graded sizes, from match to thumb thickness.
Plan the fuel wood (wrist thickness), only dead wood picked up from the ground.
Gather twice as much of each category as seems necessary, BEFORE lighting.
attention: Never cut living branches: they don't burn and it is forbidden.
feu.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

tipi.intro: The simplest structure to start with: the flame rises and catches the wood above.
etapes: Put the tinder in a ball in the centre.
Stand the finest kindling in a cone around it, leaving an opening on the wind side.
Light the tinder through the opening, at ground level.
Blow gently at the base when the flames catch.
Add bigger and bigger wood without crushing the structure.
tipi.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

cabane.intro: Burns for a long time and gives a fine bed of embers, ideal for cooking.
etapes: Start a small teepee in the centre.
Lay two parallel logs on each side, then two more across on top, like a log cabin.
Build 3 to 5 layers, slightly reducing the size towards the top.
Let the fire collapse into embers before putting the pot on.
cabane.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

ferro.intro: A fire steel works wet, in severe cold and thousands of times. It belongs in every bivouac pack.
etapes: Prepare a nest of very fine, dry tinder (grated birch bark, cotton, shavings).
Put the tip of the rod IN the tinder, striker pressed at about 45°.
Pull the rod towards you rather than pushing the striker: you won't scatter the nest.
Repeat firmly until the sparks catch, then blow gently.
attention: Sparks exceed 3,000 °C: keep fingers and synthetic clothing away.
ferro.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

feupluie.intro: In wet weather, in autumn and winter, everything is wet. You have to look for dry material where it hides.
etapes: Gather dead twigs still on the tree, at the bottom of spruces: they stay dry under the branches.
Take birch bark from dead trees or from the ground.
Split pieces of dead wood: the heart stays dry even when the outside is soaked.
Build a platform of sticks on the wet ground and light the fire on it.
Shelter the starting fire with your body or a high tarp, never right over the flames.
attention: Never light a fire under a tent or a closed tarp: risk of fire and carbon monoxide.
feupluie.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

froid.intro: In autumn and winter, nights near 0 °C and damp. Cold and wet together are the real danger of bivouacking.
etapes: Stay dry: change before you get cold, keep a dry outfit for the night only.
Layering system: breathable base (no cotton), warm layer, waterproof shell.
Insulate from the ground: at rest, you lose a large part of your heat into it. A good mat matters as much as the sleeping bag.
Eat and drink something hot before sleeping.
Warning signs: uncontrollable shivering, clumsy movements, confusion. Warm the person and call 112 if it gets worse.
attention: Someone who stops shivering while still cold is in danger: call the emergency services.
froid.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

abri.intro: A good spot is half of a good night.
etapes: Only on an authorised bivouac area or private land with permission (see the Map tab).
Look up: no dead branch or dead tree above you.
Avoid the valley bottom and the very edge of the river: cold air, damp, possible rising water.
Look for a dry, slightly raised ledge, close to dead wood and water.
Turn the shelter's entrance away from the prevailing wind.
abri.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

bache.intro: The quickest with gear: a 3 × 3 m tarp and 10 m of cord.
etapes: Stretch a cord between two trees, from hip to shoulder height depending on the weather (lower = warmer).
Drape the tarp over the cord.
Peg the four corners to the ground, sides well tensioned so the rain runs off.
Line the ground with dry leaves or needles under the mat.
attention: Tie a little piece of string onto the cord on each side: water drips off it instead of running into the shelter.
bache.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

appentis.intro: A sloping roof open on one side, effective with a reflected fire in front (where fires are allowed).
etapes: Wedge a strong ridgepole between two trees, at chest height.
Lean poles against it, on the wind side, at about 45°, 30 cm apart.
Weave flexible branches across them to form a grid.
Cover with leafy branches, ferns or leaves, from the bottom up like roof tiles.
Insulate the ground with a thick layer of dry leaves.
attention: Only with dead wood and on land where it is allowed.
appentis.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

debris.intro: The warmest survival shelter without gear: a giant sleeping bag of dead leaves.
etapes: Find a ridgepole about 1.5 times your height.
Rest one end on a stump or tripod at knee height, the other on the ground.
Lay branches along both sides, close together, to form ribs.
Cover with small branches then a layer of dead leaves 60 cm to 1 m thick (an arm's length).
Fill the inside with dry leaves, go in feet first and block the entrance with a pile of leaves.
attention: The inside must be just big enough for you: the smaller, the warmer.
debris.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

orientation.intro: In valleys or forests, mobile signal is often patchy.
etapes: Before leaving: study the route and display it in the Map tab to keep it cached.
Following a river downstream leads sooner or later to a village or a road.
The sun is due south around the middle of the day: between 12 and 1 pm in winter time, between 1 and 2 pm in summer time (Western Europe).
With an analogue watch: point the hour hand at the sun. South is halfway between it and 12 (1 in summer time).
orientation.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

baton.intro: Find east and west with a simple stick, as soon as there is a little sun.
etapes: Plant a straight stick in flat ground.
Mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble: that is WEST.
Wait 15 minutes and mark the new tip of the shadow: that is EAST.
The line between the two marks runs west to east. A perpendicular gives north and south.
baton.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

polaire.intro: The North Star shows north to within about 1°, all year round in the northern hemisphere.
etapes: Find the Plough (Big Dipper), the “saucepan” of 7 bright stars.
Take the two stars on the edge of the pan, opposite the handle.
Extend their line by about 5 times the gap between them.
The fairly bright, isolated star you reach is the North Star: it shows north.
polaire.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

urgence.intro: 112 goes through any available mobile network, even if it isn't your operator's.
etapes: Call 112 and give your GPS coordinates (crisis button in the middle of the app).
If the call doesn't go through, send an SMS to a loved one with your position, then climb higher to look for signal.
Stay put if someone knows where you are: a person who stays still is found faster.
Always tell someone your route and return time before you leave.
urgence.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

signaux.intro: Anything repeated three times means “distress”, all over the world.
etapes: Whistle: 3 long blasts, a pause, and repeat. It carries much further than the voice and is less tiring.
Light: 3 repeated flashes, or SOS (3 short, 3 long, 3 short).
Fires: 3 fires in a triangle about thirty metres apart, in a clearing visible from the sky (if the situation requires).
On the ground, symbols at least 4 × 6 m in branches or stones: V = need help, X = need medical assistance (see the Ground-to-air codes sheet).
Wear a bright colour and spread it out in an open place.
attention: In the mountains, the Alpine distress signal is 6 signals a minute, then a minute's pause.
signaux.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

piege.titre: Survival traps: what you need to know
piege.intro: Military manuals describe snares and deadfalls (like the “figure 4” trap). In Belgium as in France, setting them is poaching, except in a real life-threatening emergency.
etapes: On a bivouac of a few days, food is never the priority: bring your own.
In a real emergency, favour what takes little energy: foraging for plants identified with certainty (Species tab).
Traps only work if you set many of them on active runs (paths, tracks, droppings) and check them often.
A forgotten trap keeps killing: in a real situation, dismantle them all before leaving.
attention: Forbidden outside a life-threatening emergency: fines and prosecution for poaching.
Fishing requires a licence (fishing licence in Wallonia, fishing card in France…).
piege.source: US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

traces.intro: This is what allows bivouac areas to stay open.
etapes: Take all your rubbish away, including food waste and toilet paper.
Toilet: more than 50 m from water, in a 15 cm hole filled back in.
No soap in the river, even biodegradable.
Arrive late, leave early, stay discreet, leave the place cleaner than you found it.

chaise.intro: THE fixed loop: it doesn't slip and is easy to untie after loading. To tie a rope to a tree or make a rescue loop around the waist.
etapes: Make a small loop in the standing part (the “rabbit hole”), the working end passing over the top.
Pass the working end up through the small loop from underneath: “the rabbit comes out of the hole”.
Pass it behind the standing part: “it goes round the tree”.
Bring it back down through the small loop: “it goes back down the hole”.
Tighten by holding the working end and the big loop, then pull the standing part. Leave a tail of at least 10 cm.
attention: It can loosen when not loaded: secure the tail with a half hitch.
chaise.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

tendeur.intro: The guyline knot: it slides to adjust tension and locks under load. Ideal for tensioning a tarp or tent.
etapes: Pass the cord around the peg or tree.
With the working end, make two turns around the standing part, working towards the peg (inside the loop).
Make a third turn around the standing part, this time outside the first two.
Tighten: slide the knot to tension or slacken.
attention: On very slippery cord (Dyneema), add one more turn on the inside.
tendeur.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

cabestan.intro: Quick for fixing a rope to a pole or peg, and the starting point of all lashings.
etapes: Make a full turn around the pole.
Cross over the standing part and make a second turn beside the first.
Tuck the working end under this second turn, between the pole and the rope.
Tighten by pulling the two ends in opposite directions.
attention: It can slip if the support turns: add a half hitch for safety.
cabestan.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

tourmort.titre: Round turn and two half hitches
tourmort.intro: A strong mooring of a rope to a tree, easy to untie even after a heavy load. Perfect for a ridgeline.
etapes: Make two full turns around the tree (the “round turn” takes the strain).
Tie a half hitch around the standing part.
Tie a second half hitch in the same direction as the first.
Push the hitches up against the round turn and tighten.
tourmort.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

camionneur.intro: An improvised pulley that doubles the force: to tension a ridgeline like a guitar string.
etapes: Tie one end to the first tree (round turn and two half hitches).
Towards the second tree, form a fixed loop in the rope (figure-eight loop or a locked slip loop): that is the “pulley”.
Pass the working end around the second tree, come back and thread it through the loop.
Pull the working end towards the tree: the tension increases sharply.
Lock it with two half hitches just below the loop.
attention: Don't over-tighten on a weak branch or a dead tree.
camionneur.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

huit.intro: The standard stopper knot at the end of a rope, and, tied in a doubled rope, a very safe fixed loop (figure-eight loop).
etapes: Make a loop with the working end.
Pass the working end around the standing part.
Tuck it through the loop from above: the rope forms an “8”.
Tighten. For a loop: double the rope and tie exactly the same knot with the doubled part.
huit.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

plat.intro: For tying the two ends of a bandage, a bag or a bundle. Not for joining two ropes that bear a load.
etapes: Cross the left end over the right and tuck it under (first overhand).
Cross the right end over the left and tuck it under (second overhand).
Check that each end comes out on the same side as its own rope: the knot is flat and symmetrical.
Tighten.
attention: If the ends come out at an angle, it's a “granny knot” that slips: tie it again.
Never for climbing or rescue.
plat.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

ecoute.intro: Joins two ropes, even of different diameters. For lengthening a rope that is too short.
etapes: Form a U (a bight) with the end of the thicker rope.
Pass the end of the thinner rope up through the U from underneath.
Take it round behind both strands of the U.
Tuck it under itself, without going through the U.
Tighten: both free ends must come out on the same side.
attention: For extra security, make two turns instead of one: double sheet bend.
ecoute.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)
